newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians prepare for key general election.
newsitem.headline: Albanians prepare for key general election.

text.p: Albania's main political parties wound up their hard-fought campaigns and prepared for Sunday's first round of an early general election called to halt the nation's slide into chaos.

Both President Sali Berisha's dominant Democratic Party and its main rival, the Socialists,ended their campaigns on Friday with rallies on Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square. Their messages were almost the same: to deliver Albania from the violence that has swept the country after the collapse of shady investment funds.
The election was called as part of a pact struck at the height of the disturbances in March to set up an interim unity government made up of 10 parties.

The vote is being held 13 months after the Democrats won a big victory in Albania's third multi-party elections since the collapse of communism in 1990. International observers said that vote was subject to manipulation and voter intimidation.

But as some 500 international observers working under the the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) took off for their pre-assigned positions on Friday, there was little hope Sunday's poll would be free of difficulties.
OSCE special envoy Franz Vranitzky has said the polls are being held in unusual circumstances and would be complex -- a state of emergency imposed on March 2 is still in force.
At least 1,500 people have been killed in four months of unrest after hundreds of thousands of Albanians lost their live savings when five pyramid investment funds folded.
Most of them blamed Berisha's government for their losses, but the Democrats say the Socialists incited the violence.
The south, the focus of the unrest, remains outside the government's control and is largely ruled by armed gangs.
Some 7,000 soldiers despatched to Albania as part of an Italian-dominated security force have helped to keep a lid on looting and destruction.
But few believe that order will return once the ballots are counted and the OSCE has delivered its verdict on the fairness of the election early next week.
"It would be fair to say already that there are several areas in which it would be difficult to say that this is a normal election," OSCE election coordinator Tony Welch said.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in a message read on the Voice of America, urged Albanians to turn out to vote "to chart a better future for your country".
"The gesture of voting is a very important one for me, for I have witnessed societies where this right was not allowed," Albright, born in pre-war Czechoslovakia, said.

Berisha has pledged to restore order to the country of 3.4 million within 75 days. Democratic Party officials predict they will win around 50 percent of the vote but hint they may be prepared to become the official opposition if the leftists win.
The constitutional court ruled late on Friday the 4,525 voting stations should close at 6 p.m. rather than at 9 p.m. as originally planned, and open one hour ahead of scheduled at 7 a.m.
Political parties and the OSCE had called for the opening hours to be cut for the sake of safety.

But regardless of the outcome, Western observers remain concerned whether the leading parties will respect the vote. Both complain that they have been prevented from campaigning in some areas by rival supporters.

Sources close to Berisha, who insists he will accept the results if backed by the OSCE, have told diplomats privately that he will step down if the left wins power. But if the vote is close, he will probably remain.
"I think it will be fairly close and with Berisha in power it'll be difficult for Albania to move ahead," one envoy said.
